text: You’re at the bedside. The blood pressure has fallen after intubation. Before you reach for fluid, build the physiology in your head. Picture the right ventricle pushing against the pulmonary circulation. Positive pressure has changed venous return, pulmonary vascular resistance, and the pressure surrounding the heart. Your job is not to chase a number. Your job is to decide what changed, predict what your intervention should do, and then watch whether the patient proves your model right.

Your pulse oximeter says ninety-eight percent. That feels reassuring. But saturation answers a very specific question: what fraction of the available hemoglobin binding sites are carrying oxygen? It does not tell you how much hemoglobin you have, and it does not tell you how much blood the heart is moving. That distinction is the beginning of oxygen-delivery thinking. Oxygen delivery, D O 2, is cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content. Arterial oxygen content is dominated by oxygen bound to hemoglobin. A useful bedside approximation is one point three four times hemoglobin times arterial saturation, plus a very small contribution from oxygen dissolved in plasma. That means three patients can all have an S P O 2 of ninety-eight percent and have very different oxygen delivery. Picture the first patient. Hemoglobin fourteen. Cardiac output five liters per minute. Saturation ninety-eight percent. Nothing surprising. Now keep saturation at ninety-eight percent but drop the hemoglobin to five. Every remaining red cell may be beautifully saturated, but there are far fewer red cells carrying oxygen. The pulse oximeter still looks excellent while arterial oxygen content has fallen dramatically. Now take a different patient. Hemoglobin is normal. Saturation is ninety-eight percent. But cardiac output has collapsed because of severe pump failure. The blood contains plenty of oxygen per deciliter, but not enough blood is reaching the tissues each minute. Again, the pulse oximeter can look perfect. This is why expert critical-care reasoning does not ask only, “Is the blood oxygenated?” It asks, “Is enough oxygen actually being delivered?” Now add the tissues. Oxygen consumption, V O 2, is what the body removes from the delivered oxygen. When delivery falls, tissues can initially compensate by extracting a larger fraction. Venous oxygen saturation falls because more oxygen is being taken out before the blood returns to the right heart. That compensation has limits. Below a critical level of delivery, oxygen consumption can become supply dependent. Do not turn that into another single-number rule. A low venous saturation can reflect low cardiac output, anemia, increased metabolic demand, arterial hypoxemia, or combinations of them. A surprisingly high venous saturation can occur when extraction is impaired or when flow distribution is abnormal. The number only becomes useful when it sits inside a physiologic model. Here is the mental shortcut I want you to keep. Saturation tells you how full the buses are. Hemoglobin tells you how many buses you have. Cardiac output tells you how fast the buses are moving. Oxygen delivery asks how many passengers actually arrive each minute. So the next time you see an S P O 2 of ninety-eight percent in a patient who looks poorly perfused, do not let the monitor end the conversation. Ask about hemoglobin. Ask about flow. Ask what the tissues are extracting. Ask whether the patient is warm or cold, alert or altered, making urine or shutting down, clearing lactate or accumulating it. A normal saturation can coexist with profoundly inadequate oxygen delivery. Your retrieval question is this: if saturation stays the same, name the two major variables that can still make oxygen delivery collapse. The answer is hemoglobin and cardiac output. And the expert move is not merely remembering the formula. It is noticing when the patient and the pulse oximeter are telling different stories.

You're listening to ICU Literacy: transmural pressure. The pressure that actually distends a chamber is not always the number on the monitor. This is a level 4 critical-care session. The goal is not to memorize a list. The goal is to build a model that lets you predict what the patient will do next. By the end, you should be able to use transmural pressure to explain why measured filling pressures change with intrathoracic pressure. Now: Inside pressure minus outside pressure. Preload. The loading conditions of a ventricle before contraction; not synonymous with a single pressure or volume. Build the mechanism first. Preload is the myocardial fiber-loading condition before contraction. It is influenced by venous return, ventricular compliance, pericardial pressure and intrathoracic pressure, so a measured filling pressure is only an imperfect surrogate. At the bedside, interpret filling pressure together with volume response, congestion, ventricular geometry and the pressure surrounding the heart. A CVP of 14 can mean very different things in RV failure, tamponade and positive-pressure ventilation. Two traps to actively avoid: Equating CVP with circulating volume. And: Assuming fluid responsiveness means fluid is indicated or tolerated. The integration move is this: Ask what changed the effective distending pressure of the ventricle, not merely what changed the monitor number. Keep these terms available in your mental model: end-diastolic volume, transmural pressure. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Distinguish preload from CVP or fluid responsiveness. Predict how changes in intrathoracic pressure alter measured filling pressures. Positive-pressure ventilation & circulation. Positive intrathoracic pressure changes venous return, ventricular transmural pressures and pulmonary vascular resistance. Build the mechanism first. Positive intrathoracic pressure can reduce the gradient for venous return, change transmural ventricular pressures and alter P V R depending on lung volume and recruitability. At the bedside, post-intubation hypotension may reflect vasodilation, reduced venous return, increased RV afterload, auto-peep or previously compensated shock becoming unmasked. Two traps to actively avoid: Attributing every post-intubation pressure drop to induction medication. And: Assuming positive pressure has a single predictable effect on both ventricles. The integration move is this: Think preload, RV afterload and LV transmural afterload separately. Keep these terms available in your mental model: transmural pressure, mean airway pressure. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Predict why induction and positive pressure can precipitate hypotension. Distinguish effects on RV preload, RV afterload and LV transmural afterload. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Before you finish, retrieve the model without looking at notes. Can you use transmural pressure to explain why measured filling pressures change with intrathoracic pressure? If any part still feels like a memorized phrase instead of a mechanism you can predict with, that is the part to review next.

This is a level 4 critical-care session. The goal is not to memorize a list. The goal is to build a model that lets you predict what the patient will do next. By the end, you should be able to phenotype mixed shock and choose a testable physiologic intervention rather than reflexively treating a pressure. Now: Stop naming shock by one number. Shock phenotyping. Identify inadequate effective circulation by integrating flow, vascular tone, congestion, oxygen delivery and organ response. Build the mechanism first. Shock is inadequate effective tissue perfusion and oxygen utilization, not merely hypotension. Flow, vascular tone, capacitance, congestion and extraction can fail in different combinations. At the bedside, phenotype the circulation repeatedly. A patient can move from one dominant mechanism to another during resuscitation. Two traps to actively avoid: Naming shock once and never revisiting the model. And: Treating MAP as the only endpoint. The integration move is this: Choose interventions that both treat the suspected mechanism and generate information about whether the model was correct. Keep these terms available in your mental model: flow, tone, congestion, perfusion. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Recognize mixed shock. Choose an intervention that tests a physiologic hypothesis and define the response expected if that hypothesis is correct. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Now: Flow and venous return. Venous return. Flow back to the right heart determined by the pressure gradient from the systemic circulation and resistance to venous return. Build the mechanism first. Venous return depends on the pressure gradient from the systemic venous reservoir toward the right atrium and on resistance to that flow. Mean systemic filling pressure and right-atrial pressure can move independently. At the bedside, a rise in right-atrial pressure can reduce venous return even when the patient appears more “full.” Venoconstriction can recruit unstressed volume and change the upstream pressure without adding external fluid. Two traps to actively avoid: Treating a high CVP as proof of adequate forward flow. And: Ignoring abdominal, thoracic or pericardial pressure as downstream resistance. The integration move is this: Predict how fluid, venoconstriction, peep and RV failure each alter the venous-return gradient. Keep these terms available in your mental model: mean systemic filling pressure, stressed volume, venous return gradient. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Explain why CVP can rise while venous return falls. Predict effects of vasodilation, venoconstriction and positive pressure on venous return. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Now: Delivery and extraction. Oxygen delivery. DO2 is cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content; saturation alone does not describe tissue oxygen delivery. Build the mechanism first. Oxygen delivery equals cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, which is dominated by hemoglobin-bound oxygen rather than dissolved oxygen. At the bedside, normal saturation can coexist with critically low delivery in severe anemia or low-flow shock. Ask about hemoglobin and flow whenever tissue perfusion looks worse than the pulse oximeter. Two traps to actively avoid: Using SpO2 as a proxy for whole-body oxygen delivery. And: Forgetting that raising saturation from already-high levels adds little content. The integration move is this: Saturation tells you how full the carriers are; hemoglobin tells you how many carriers exist; cardiac output tells you how fast they move. Keep these terms available in your mental model: CaO2, DO2, VO2. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Predict effects of hemoglobin, saturation and flow on oxygen delivery. Explain why a normal SpO2 can coexist with inadequate DO2. Oxygen extraction. The relationship between delivered and consumed oxygen reflected by venous saturation and tissue extraction. Build the mechanism first. Tissues can increase extraction when delivery falls, lowering venous oxygen saturation until extraction reserve is exhausted. High venous saturation can also be abnormal when extraction is impaired or flow is maldistributed. At the bedside, interpret SvO2 or ScvO2 alongside cardiac output, hemoglobin, arterial saturation, metabolic demand and shock phenotype. Two traps to actively avoid: Calling a high venous saturation reassuring in every patient. And: Treating low venous saturation as a diagnosis instead of a physiologic clue. You're listening to Audio Case: A R D S + RV failure. An unfolding multisystem case with no clean single-organ answer. This is a level 5 critical-care session. The goal is not to memorize a list. The goal is to build a model that lets you predict what the patient will do next. By the end, you should be able to balance lung recruitment and rv load while explicitly stating uncertainty and tradeoffs. Now: The handoff. A R D S physiology. Diffuse inflammatory lung injury producing heterogeneity, shunt, low aerated lung volume and risk from ventilator-induced injury. Build the mechanism first. A R D S produces heterogeneous inflammatory lung injury, shunt, edema and a reduced aerated “baby lung,” making regional overdistension possible even at seemingly modest tidal volumes. At the bedside, integrate gas exchange, compliance, recruitability, prone response, driving pressure and hemodynamics rather than treating the P/F ratio alone. Two traps to actively avoid: Equating severe hypoxemia with universal recruitability. And: Improving oxygenation at the cost of excessive distending pressure or RV load. The integration move is this: A R D S management is a tradeoff between oxygenation, mechanical injury and circulation. Keep these terms available in your mental model: baby lung, shunt, recruitability. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Integrate oxygenation, mechanics, recruitability and hemodynamics rather than treating a P/F ratio in isolation. Right ventricular failure. Failure of a thin-walled ventricle that is highly sensitive to acute afterload, volume, perfusion pressure and ventricular interaction. Build the mechanism first. The RV is thin-walled and highly sensitive to acute afterload. When it dilates, wall stress rises, coronary perfusion can fall and septal shift can reduce LV filling. At the bedside, track systemic pressure, venous congestion, echo geometry, oxygenation, CO2, acid-base status and ventilator pressures together. Small changes in P V R or intrathoracic pressure can have large hemodynamic consequences. Two traps to actively avoid: Reflexively giving fluid to every hypotensive RV patient. And: Focusing on systemic pressure while ignoring worsening RV dilation and congestion. The integration move is this: Every intervention should be judged by its effects on RV preload, RV afterload, contractility and coronary perfusion. Keep these terms available in your mental model: RV-PA coupling, septal shift, transmural pressure. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Recognize RV shock physiology before systemic hypotension becomes profound. Predict how peep, hypercapnia, hypoxemia, fluids and vasoactives may change RV performance. Pause here and answer this before you continue: Before more data arrives, what are your competing priorities? Do not grade yourself only on whether you found the expected answer. Ask whether your reasoning predicted a physiologic response and what evidence would make you change your mind. Now: The vent becomes part of the circulation. peep. Positive end-expiratory pressure used to preserve recruitment and oxygenation, with important mechanical and hemodynamic effects. Build the mechanism first. peep can prevent end-expiratory collapse and recruit unstable lung units, but can also overdistend already-open units and transmit pressure to the thorax. At the bedside, judge a peep change by oxygenation, compliance, driving pressure, hemodynamics and the disease’s recruitability rather than by oxygen saturation alone. Two traps to actively avoid: Chasing oxygenation while ignoring falling cardiac output. And: Assuming higher peep is either universally protective or universally harmful. The integration move is this: The useful peep is the one that improves the whole patient, not just the alveolar oxygen number. Keep these terms available in your mental model: recruitability, intrinsic peep. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Explain when increasing peep may recruit lung versus overdistend it. Anticipate circulatory effects in preload-dependent or RV-failing patients. Pulmonary vascular resistance. Resistance faced by the RV, influenced by lung volume, oxygenation, CO2, pH, pulmonary vascular disease and mechanical ventilation. Build the mechanism first. Pulmonary vascular resistance reflects the combined behavior of alveolar and extra-alveolar vessels and is affected by lung volume, oxygen, CO2, pH and pulmonary vascular disease. At the bedside, both severe derecruitment and overdistension can raise RV afterload. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia and acidosis can compound the problem. Two traps to actively avoid: Assuming more peep always lowers P V R by recruiting lung. And: Ignoring gas chemistry as an RV afterload intervention. The integration move is this: Interpret ventilator changes through both lung mechanics and the pulmonary circulation. Keep these terms available in your mental model: RV afterload, West zones. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Explain the U-shaped relationship between lung volume and pulmonary vascular resistance. Identify reversible contributors to acute RV afterload. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Now: The RV is telling you something. Right ventricular failure. And: Focusing on systemic pressure while ignoring worsening RV dilation and congestion. The integration move is this: Every intervention should be judged by its effects on RV preload, RV afterload, contractility and coronary perfusion. Keep these terms available in your mental model: RV-PA coupling, septal shift, transmural pressure. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Recognize RV shock physiology before systemic hypotension becomes profound. Predict how peep, hypercapnia, hypoxemia, fluids and vasoactives may change RV performance. Ventricular interdependence. The ventricles share a septum and constrained pericardial space, so pressure or volume loading of one changes filling and geometry of the other. Build the mechanism first. The ventricles share a septum and a constrained pericardial space. Acute RV pressure or volume loading can shift the septum and reduce LV diastolic filling. At the bedside, a falling LV stroke volume in RV failure may occur despite apparently adequate intravascular volume because geometry, not supply, is limiting filling. Two traps to actively avoid: Treating LV output and RV function as separate systems. And: Calling septal flattening a descriptive echo finding without hemodynamic meaning. The integration move is this: When one ventricle enlarges or its pressure rises, ask what that does to the other ventricle’s filling conditions. Keep these terms available in your mental model: septal shift, pericardial constraint. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Use septal position and loading conditions to explain falling LV output during RV distension. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Now: There is no free intervention. Multisystem treatment tradeoffs. A therapy that helps one organ can worsen another; expert care weighs global benefit, reversibility and monitoring. Build the mechanism first. Organ-support interventions frequently redistribute risk: peep can help oxygenation but worsen RV load; fluids can increase flow but worsen congestion; sedation can improve synchrony but obscure neurologic assessment. At the bedside, before intervening, name the intended benefit, the organ/system at risk and the signal that would tell you the tradeoff has become unfavorable. Two traps to actively avoid: Optimizing one organ in isolation. And: Treating guideline targets as independent goals that can all be maximized simultaneously. The integration move is this: Expert critical care is often choosing the least harmful global strategy rather than a perfect organ-specific intervention. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Explain at least two competing organ effects of a proposed intervention. Choose the least harmful testable strategy when the optimal answer is uncertain. Pause here and answer this before you continue: Choose your next move and name the organ you could worsen. Do not grade yourself only on whether you found the expected answer. Ask whether your reasoning predicted a physiologic response and what evidence would make you change your mind. Before you finish, retrieve the model without looking at notes. Can you balance lung recruitment and RV load while explicitly stating uncertainty and tradeoffs? If any part still feels like a memorized phrase instead of a mechanism you can predict with, that is the part to review next.

High-risk medication safety. Use standardized concentration, labeling, independent verification, closed-loop communication and context checks for high-risk drugs. Build the mechanism first. High-risk medication harm often arises from system failures: concentration mismatch, unlabeled syringes, look-alike products, route errors and communication breakdowns. You're listening to The physiologically difficult airway. R S I preparation, positive-pressure transition and the first five minutes after the tube. This is a level 5 critical-care session. The goal is not to memorize a list. The goal is to build a model that lets you predict what the patient will do next. By the end, you should be able to identify physiologic risk before induction; and run the post-intubation period as active resuscitation rather than a checklist afterthought. Now: Why the patient may not tolerate apnea or induction. R S I preparation & peri-intubation physiology. R S I is a physiologic resuscitation that includes preoxygenation, hemodynamic preparation, drug strategy, positioning, backup planning and post-intubation care. Build the mechanism first. R S I changes oxygenation, ventilation, sympathetic tone and intrathoracic pressure abruptly. Physiologically difficult airways fail because the circulation or gas exchange cannot tolerate that transition. At the bedside, prepare oxygenation, hemodynamics, suction, primary/backup devices, rescue ventilation and post-intubation support before induction. Two traps to actively avoid: Treating R S I as laryngoscopy plus drugs. And: Ignoring severe RV failure, metabolic acidosis or shock until after apnea begins. The integration move is this: The airway procedure includes the minutes before and after tube passage. Keep these terms available in your mental model: preoxygenation, apneic oxygenation, first-pass success, peri-intubation arrest. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Identify physiologically difficult airways before induction. Build an airway plan that includes hemodynamics and the first five minutes after tube placement. Right ventricular failure. Failure of a thin-walled ventricle that is highly sensitive to acute afterload, volume, perfusion pressure and ventricular interaction. Build the mechanism first. The RV is thin-walled and highly sensitive to acute afterload. When it dilates, wall stress rises, coronary perfusion can fall and septal shift can reduce LV filling. At the bedside, track systemic pressure, venous congestion, echo geometry, oxygenation, CO2, acid-base status and ventilator pressures together. Small changes in P V R or intrathoracic pressure can have large hemodynamic consequences. Two traps to actively avoid: Reflexively giving fluid to every hypotensive RV patient. And: Focusing on systemic pressure while ignoring worsening RV dilation and congestion. The integration move is this: Every intervention should be judged by its effects on RV preload, RV afterload, contractility and coronary perfusion. Keep these terms available in your mental model: RV-PA coupling, septal shift, transmural pressure. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Recognize RV shock physiology before systemic hypotension becomes profound. Predict how peep, hypercapnia, hypoxemia, fluids and vasoactives may change RV performance. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Now: The circulation changes when positive pressure starts. Positive-pressure ventilation & circulation. Positive intrathoracic pressure changes venous return, ventricular transmural pressures and pulmonary vascular resistance. Build the mechanism first. Positive intrathoracic pressure can reduce the gradient for venous return, change transmural ventricular pressures and alter P V R depending on lung volume and recruitability. At the bedside, post-intubation hypotension may reflect vasodilation, reduced venous return, increased RV afterload, auto-peep or previously compensated shock becoming unmasked. Two traps to actively avoid: Attributing every post-intubation pressure drop to induction medication. And: Assuming positive pressure has a single predictable effect on both ventricles. The integration move is this: Think preload, RV afterload and LV transmural afterload separately. Keep these terms available in your mental model: transmural pressure, mean airway pressure. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Predict why induction and positive pressure can precipitate hypotension. Distinguish effects on RV preload, RV afterload and LV transmural afterload. Tie this back to the patient. Ask what variable is changing, what downstream effect you expect, and what bedside finding would support or contradict that model. Now: Confirmation is only the midpoint. Post-intubation stabilization. Tube confirmation is the beginning of post-intubation care: oxygenation, ventilation, hemodynamics, sedation, ventilator setup and diagnosis must be reassessed together. Build the mechanism first. Intubation creates a new physiologic state: airway resistance, mean intrathoracic pressure, sedation, ventilation and venous return all change at once. At the bedside, confirm tube with waveform capnography, set disease-appropriate ventilation, establish analgesia/sedation and reassess hypotension or hypoxemia mechanistically. Two traps to actively avoid: Declaring success at tube confirmation. And: Forgetting analgesia/sedation in a paralyzed patient. The integration move is this: The first five minutes determine whether airway control becomes physiologic rescue or a new source of instability. Keep these terms available in your mental model: waveform capnography, post-intubation hypotension, analgosedation. What expert-level use of this concept looks like is this: Run a reproducible first-five-minutes stabilization sequence. Treat hypotension or hypoxemia as a physiology problem rather than simply changing one ventilator or medication setting. Tie this back to the patient. Ventilator emergency troubleshooting. A structured patient-to-device approach to acute hypoxemia, high pressure, low pressure, dyssynchrony and post-intubation deterioration. Build the mechanism first. Acute ventilator deterioration can originate from the patient, tube, circuit or machine. Peak and plateau pressures help separate resistance from compliance when measurements are trustworthy. At the bedside, look at the patient first, rescue oxygenation/ventilation if the device cannot be trusted, then trace from patient to tube to circuit to machine. Two traps to actively avoid: Staring at the ventilator while the patient deteriorates. And: Treating every high-pressure alarm as bronchospasm. You are at the bedside. The pressure is falling and you have decided a short bridge is needed while definitive support is prepared. Before touching a vial, state the physiologic problem you are treating.

High-risk medication errors happen when urgency outruns verification. Separate the patient decision from the preparation task. Read the source concentration. Read your protocol. Do not build the final concentration from memory alone.
Picture the syringe, label, medication source and reference in one uncluttered field. Keep look-alike syringes out of that field. Prepare only one high-risk drug at a time.
Before administration, verify drug, concentration, dose, route, patient and indication. Say them out loud. If the concentration does not match the standard you expected, stop and reconcile it.

Give according to local protocol through a verified line. Your attention immediately returns to the patient and monitor. Watch rhythm, pressure, perfusion and the clinical endpoint you named before the dose.
If the response is excessive, absent or physiologically inconsistent, do not automatically repeat the same action. Recheck the line, concentration, rhythm and your diagnosis.

The mental anchor is simple: indication, standardized concentration, verify, label, administer, reassess, and transition to definitive support. The procedure is not drawing up a syringe. The procedure is safe physiology-guided medication use.
Before you spike anything, name what you are treating: oxygen-carrying capacity, hemorrhagic shock, a component deficiency, or a specific protocol target.
Pause over the product and the patient. Perform the required patient, product, compatibility and expiration checks exactly as your system requires. This is a deliberate interruption, not paperwork.

Picture the approved blood tubing and filter, compatible carrier fluid if required by policy, warming equipment when indicated, patent vascular access, and monitoring already running before the product starts.
Begin according to policy and stay clinically present. Reassess the patient, not only the pump. A reaction can begin with subtle symptoms before the monitor changes.

New fever, chills, dyspnea, pain, hypotension, rash or a sense that something is wrong demands immediate reassessment and the local transfusion-reaction process. Do not explain away a new change simply because the patient was already sick.
Indication. Identity. Product. Circuit. Patient. Early reassessment. Reaction recognition. Documentation and response. Every time.
You need beat-to-beat pressure and arterial sampling. Picture the patient positioned, monitoring visible, rescue equipment available and the entire pressure system prepared before puncture.
Visualize the artery in cross-section and long axis. If ultrasound is used, keep the actual needle tip in view rather than following a bright shaft and assuming the tip is there.
Mentally trace catheter to tubing, flush system, pressure source, transducer, cable and monitor. An excellent puncture connected to a poor monitoring system gives poor data.

Level the transducer to the reference point used by your unit, zero to atmosphere, then restore the system to the patient. Understand what happens to displayed pressure when the transducer is too high or too low.
Do not accept a number without its waveform. Look at upstroke, systolic peak, dicrotic notch, diastolic runoff and respiratory variation in context.

When the trace looks suspicious, use the dynamic response test and inspect the circuit. Think clot, air, compliant tubing, loose connections, catheter position and excessive resonance before blaming the patient.
Patient, artery, catheter, level, zero, waveform, dynamic response. The arterial line is a measurement system, not simply a line in an artery.
You are not doing ultrasound because a probe is available. State the question: is there blood where it should not be, pericardial fluid, or pleural evidence of pneumothorax or hemothorax?
Before interpreting pathology, prove to yourself which side of the screen is cephalad, which anatomy you are seeing, and whether your probe marker matches the convention you are using.
Sweep through the hepatorenal interface, diaphragm and inferior liver tip. Do not take one frozen view and call the window negative. Search the dependent spaces.
Find spleen, kidney and diaphragm. The geometry is less forgiving. Sweep deliberately rather than chasing the textbook picture.
Use the bladder as your acoustic window and examine the dependent space around it in the appropriate planes.
Acquire the best cardiac window the patient gives you and identify the pericardial space before deciding fluid is present. Fat, pleural fluid and artifact can mislead.
Interrogate the pleural line bilaterally. Lung sliding is a dynamic sign. When absent, use the rest of the ultrasound and clinical picture rather than treating one sign as the diagnosis.
Trauma evolves. The mental anchor is orientation, systematic windows, sweeping rather than snapshotting, and repeat examination when physiology changes.
Picture the patient and state what you are treating. Tension physiology, hemothorax and ongoing pleural air are related problems but they shape urgency, equipment and aftercare differently.
See skin, subcutaneous tissue, intercostal muscles, rib, neurovascular bundle and parietal pleura. Orient to the safe procedural zone taught by your credentialing program and local policy.
The procedure includes the drain system, connections, dressing, suction or water seal plan, monitoring and analgesia strategy. Do not discover missing pieces after entering the pleural space.

Mentally rehearse deliberate tissue handling and confirmation that the pleural space has actually been entered before advancing the drain. Maintain awareness of depth and direction rather than using force.
Once connected, reassess patient physiology and the drain system together. Improvement should make physiologic sense. If nothing changes, question position, patency, diagnosis and the system.
Kinked tubing, disconnection, migration, clot, dependent loops or a new air leak can turn a functioning drain into a problem. Trace from patient outward whenever physiology worsens.
Indication, anatomy, complete setup, controlled pleural entry, connection, patient response, system response, and continuous troubleshooting.
State the indication and whether a safer or faster alternative can meet the immediate need. Prepare monitoring, sterile equipment and a plan for complications before beginning.
Identify vein and artery in more than one plane. Use compressibility, pulsatility and anatomy rather than trusting color alone. Look for overlap and thrombus.
With real-time ultrasound, keep the needle tip accounted for. A shaft crossing the ultrasound plane can look convincing while the actual tip has traveled deeper.
Do not let dark blood color alone make the decision in shock or hypoxemia. Use the confirmation method required by your environment before a dilator enters the patient.
Pass smoothly without force, maintain control of the wire, and verify that it is where you think it is. Seeing the wire in the intended vessel before dilation is a powerful safety checkpoint.
Resistance, unexpected pressure, ectopy, abnormal ultrasound position or patient deterioration are information. Stop and reconcile the anatomy before progressing.
Indication, anatomy, sterile setup, tip visibility, vessel confirmation, wire control, confirmation before dilation, then post-procedure reassessment.
The patient needs reliable vascular access now. Decide whether IO is appropriate rather than repeatedly delaying resuscitation for difficult peripheral attempts.
Picture the anatomy for the site and device you actually use. Palpate and identify the target before touching the driver.
Stabilize the limb and device, follow the device-specific technique, and stop when the expected endpoint is reached rather than adding unnecessary depth.
Assess stability, aspiration if applicable, flush behavior and the surrounding tissue. A line that does not behave as expected is not automatically usable.
Swelling, leaking, worsening pain, resistance or neurovascular change can signal extravasation or another complication. Reassess after use, not only at insertion.
Decision, landmark, device-specific placement, confirmation, securement and repeated site checks.
The patient suddenly desaturates and the ventilator is alarming. Look at the patient before the screen: chest movement, color, waveform capnography, hemodynamics and level of distress.
If oxygenation or ventilation is immediately threatened and the device cannot be trusted, transition to a reliable rescue method while troubleshooting according to your environment.
Mentally move from patient to tube to connectors to circuit to machine. Disconnection, obstruction, displacement, pneumothorax and breath stacking leave different clues.
High peak with a relatively preserved plateau points you toward resistance. High peak and high plateau point you toward compliance or pressure surrounding the lung.
Auto-PEEP, tension physiology and excessive intrathoracic pressure can present as hypotension before oxygen saturation collapses. The ventilator and circulation are one system.
Patient first. Rescue ventilation if needed. Trace the airway and circuit. Separate resistance from compliance. Look for pressure-related circulatory failure. Reassess after every intervention.
Know the ordered reference level, drainage strategy and whether the system is currently open or clamped. A drainage device without its order is an unsafe abstraction.
Visualize the reference point on the patient and the leveling device. The chamber height determines the hydrostatic threshold for drainage.
Before changing bed height or patient position, manage the drain exactly as ordered so a sudden vertical shift cannot unintentionally over-drain or stop drainage.
After the move, the old chamber position is no longer meaningful. Re-establish the patient reference and level the system again before returning it to the ordered state.
Reassess ICP waveform if monitored, drainage, neurologic state, tubing and clamps. A number that changed after repositioning may reflect the measurement system before it reflects the brain.
Order, clamp for movement as required, move, re-level to the patient, verify, then return to the prescribed drainage state.

This is not ordinary transfusion. The patient is bleeding faster than routine workflow can keep up. Activate the local hemorrhage system early enough that blood bank, access, warming and source control can move together.

Picture designated access, rapid infuser or approved delivery setup, warmer, monitoring, blood verification workflow, calcium and laboratory plan according to protocol, and someone explicitly tracking products and time.
Resuscitation buys time for source control. Continually ask where the blood is going and what definitive action ends that loss.
Temperature, ionized calcium, fibrinogen, platelet function, acid-base state and dilution can deteriorate as the resuscitation grows. Anticipate them instead of discovering them late.
Reassess mental status, pulse quality, perfusion, shock index or hemodynamics, lactate trajectory when appropriate, bleeding rate and the response to source control.
Activate early, verify products, warm everything, maintain access and monitoring, anticipate calcium/coagulation/temperature problems, and never lose sight of source control.
Before touching a needle, scan the vessel in more than one plane. Look at depth, diameter, course, compressibility and what lies underneath it.
A deep vessel may accept the needle and still lose the catheter later if too little catheter remains inside the vein. Choose equipment with the vessel depth in mind.
Advance only when you know where the true needle tip is. A bright shaft is not proof that the tip is inside the ultrasound plane.
Once the tip is convincingly intraluminal, advance enough under visualization that the catheter—not just the needle bevel—can enter the vessel.
Assess aspiration when appropriate, flush behavior, tissue response and catheter stability. Ultrasound can also help confirm that fluid is not tracking into soft tissue.
Map, choose, track the true tip, advance enough catheter, then confirm function and tissue integrity.
Before preparing drugs, define the problem you are solving: oxygenation, ventilation, airway protection, work of breathing or clinical trajectory.

Ask what induction and positive pressure will do to preload, afterload, vascular tone and the right ventricle. Severe shock, RV failure, metabolic acidosis and hypoxemia change the risk before laryngoscopy begins.
Picture primary preoxygenation, positioning, suction, apneic support when appropriate, and the rescue oxygenation strategy if first-pass success does not happen.
Primary device, backup device, bougie or adjuncts, suction, capnography, rescue ventilation and a surgical-airway pathway should exist before induction rather than after failure.
The medication plan should reflect hemodynamics, neurologic goals, bronchospasm, potassium and the expected duration of paralysis and sedation—not habit alone.
When you commit, the team should already know roles, the fallback plan and what physiology you expect to change after apnea and positive pressure.
Indication, physiology, oxygenation, equipment, rescue, medication strategy, role clarity, then induction. The airway starts before the laryngoscope.
Waveform capnography anchors tube confirmation, then clinical assessment and imaging or ultrasound when appropriate complete the picture.
Do not reflexively call it sedation. Think induction-related vasodilation, reduced venous return, increased RV afterload, occult tension physiology, auto-PEEP and the underlying shock state.
Choose a starting strategy that respects predicted body size, lung mechanics, obstructive versus restrictive physiology and the oxygenation problem.
Do not let paralysis create the illusion of comfort. Establish ongoing analgesia and sedation with explicit hemodynamic and neurologic goals.
Recheck ETCO2, oxygenation, pressure, chest mechanics, tube depth, ventilator pressures, synchrony and the response to treatment. Intubation changes the physiology you were treating.
Confirm tube, stabilize pressure, set the ventilator, sedate and analgesize, then reassess the patient as a new physiologic state.
Level, zero and inspect the pressure system before trusting a waveform. Bad measurement can create convincing but false physiology.
Picture low-pressure venous pulsations and the relationship between atrial contraction, ventricular contraction and venous filling.
Systolic pressure rises while diastolic pressure falls near zero. Ectopy during passage is information about catheter position and myocardial irritation.
Diastolic pressure steps up and a dicrotic notch appears. Now the waveform reflects pulmonary artery pressure, not RV pressure.
A valid wedge requires the correct waveform, zone conditions and minimal balloon inflation. Never treat a number that does not look physiologically real.
Combine RA, PA, wedge, cardiac output and venous saturation with the patient and trend. Use the catheter to test a model, not to collect targets.
Level and zero, recognize each chamber, validate wedge, then integrate pressures, flow and oxygen extraction as one physiologic story.
Before looking at the machine, decide what you are trying to control: solute, acid-base, potassium, volume, or several at once.
Picture access blood leaving the patient, passing the pump and filter, then returning through the venous limb. Every access, filter and return pressure reflects resistance somewhere along that path.

Dialysate creates diffusive clearance across the membrane. Replacement fluid and ultrafiltration shape convective clearance and hemoconcentration. The mode is just a combination of these transport mechanisms.
Total effluent includes therapy fluids leaving the circuit; net patient ultrafiltration is the fluid balance intervention. Keep those concepts separate.
Access pressure, return pressure, transmembrane pressure and filter pressure point to different places in the circuit. Interpret the pattern before repeatedly silencing the machine.
As renal function and extracorporeal clearance change, antimicrobial and other drug exposure can change too. Delivered therapy matters more than the label on the prescription.
Goal, blood path, transport mechanism, effluent, net fluid removal, pressure pattern, and delivered dose.
VV ECMO primarily supports gas exchange. VA ECMO supports circulation and gas exchange. The cannulation configuration determines the physiologic problem the circuit can solve.
Blood can only enter the circuit if venous drainage, cannula position, volume status and surrounding pressure permit it. Poor drainage can limit everything downstream.
Pump speed is not the same as effective support. Flow depends on preload to the circuit, afterload, cannula geometry and the patient’s circulation.
Blood flow strongly influences oxygen delivery through the circuit, while sweep gas is a major lever for carbon dioxide removal.
In VA support, return flow changes arterial pressure and LV loading. In VV support, recirculation can waste apparently impressive circuit flow.
Cannula position, native heart function, native lung function, differential hypoxemia and recirculation can create a patient-circuit mismatch that no single pump number explains.
Support goal, drainage, pump, membrane lung, return, then native circulation. Follow the blood every time.
Inflation during diastole aims to augment diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion. Deflation before systole aims to reduce the pressure the LV ejects against.
Find the dicrotic notch. Inflation should occur with aortic valve closure—not during active LV ejection.
The balloon must be out of the way before the next LV ejection. Proper deflation can lower assisted end-diastolic pressure and reduce afterload.
Inflating before aortic valve closure can increase LV work by opposing late systolic ejection.
A balloon that remains inflated into systole increases afterload—the opposite of what support is meant to accomplish.
Dicrotic notch, diastolic augmentation, deflate before systole, then compare assisted and unassisted beats for the intended effect.
Start by asking whether the patient is in pain, anxious, delirious, dyssynchronous or inadequately ventilated. A deeper sedative is not the universal answer.
Set an explicit sedation target based on the clinical need—comfort and synchrony, neurologic assessment, paralysis, refractory hypoxemia or another indication.
Many analgesic and sedative strategies alter vascular tone, respiratory drive or myocardial performance. Decide what deterioration you are prepared to recognize and treat.
Neuromuscular blockade removes movement, not awareness or pain. Analgesia and sedation must already be established and maintained when paralysis is used.
Trend comfort, synchrony, hemodynamics, delirium risk and neurologic needs. Sedation should be titrated toward an explicit clinical goal.
Pain, sedation target, physiologic cost, paralysis awareness, then repeated reassessment.
Persistent seizure activity is time-dependent. Stabilization and treatment move together; do not wait for every diagnostic answer before treating ongoing convulsive status.
Position, suction, oxygenation, glucose assessment, monitoring and vascular access happen while the seizure treatment sequence begins.
Deliver the protocol-defined first-line therapy promptly and adequately rather than giving repeated ineffective fragments.
Persistent seizure after adequate first-line treatment means the treatment phase has changed. Prepare second-line therapy and escalation rather than restarting the same loop.
Refractory seizure, medication effect, hypoventilation or loss of airway protection may require airway control—but the post-intubation sedation plan must also treat ongoing seizure risk.
Persistent coma or unexplained mental status after convulsions stop should raise concern for nonconvulsive status and the need for EEG when available.
Time, stabilize, adequate first-line therapy, change phases when it fails, secure physiology when needed, and remember that seizure activity can become invisible.
